transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-27 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58 mins | HighTide Logistics discovery - surge capacity readiness

[00:00] Olivia Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Olivia from Redwood, I have Diego from our SE team with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Priya Nair (HighTide CTO): Hi Olivia, thanks. Doing well. We wanted to use this time to talk through our latency objectives and how Redwood might fit for hosted vs dedicated or private deployments.
[00:12] Diego Ramos (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Priya. Quick agenda — understand workload patterns, p95 targets, streaming requirements, and security constraints, then cover options and a benchmark plan.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng): For context, our new routing microservice emits short prompts (~60-300 tokens typically) but occasionally needs to stream longer explanations up to 800 tokens. The critical piece is that the UI expects token-by-token streaming for real-time route updates.
[00:33] Sofia Marin (Platform Eng): We see bursts — during morning dispatch windows we can hit sudden fanout of ~400 concurrent sessions across EU and NA, with token bursts up to ~150k tokens/min for a few minutes.
[00:46] Olivia Chen: Good detail — so we're talking both steady-state and short high-amplitude surges. What's your target p95?
[00:52] Priya: We want p95 end-to-end for the streaming first token to be under 150ms from our edge app to the first token arriving in the browser. That's tough. If Dedicated or Private achieves that better than Hosted, we need the numbers.
[01:06] Diego: Understood. A couple of clarifications — is the 150ms p95 requirement network-only, or do you want Redwood's inference latency to be <150ms excluding network egress?
[01:13] Priya: It's end-to-end from our app point of view. But we can split the budget: ideally we allocate ~50-70ms for inference (model runtime + tokengen), rest for networking and client rendering.
[01:23] Liam: Important note — we have edge PoPs in Dublin and Amsterdam. Data residency: EU data must stay within EU. Private or VPC is likely necessary for compliance.
[01:31] Olivia: Noted. Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) can run in your EU region and integrate with your KMS/HSM — we support customer-managed keys and audit logs. Diego, can you walk through expected token/sec numbers and tradeoffs?
[01:40] Diego: Sure. Based on sequence length distribution you described: many short requests and occasional long streams. For short 60–300 token responses with streaming, we need to consider batch size vs latency. Continuous batching helps throughput but can add to tail latency. Our Dedicated fleet with continuous batching and small max batch windows aimed at low-latency workloads often hits p95 inference of ~30–90ms for optimized 7B-ish models on A100-like instances, but numbers vary with model architecture and KV cache behavior.
[02:03] Liam: We're evaluating a quantized 13B open model — the token generation cost is higher than 7B. How will that affect p95?
[02:11] Diego: Expectedly higher. For 13B quantized on inference-optimized hardware, p95 for single-stream low-latency can be in the 60–140ms range depending on concurrent KV cache pressure. Burst concurrency will push that up if batching windows increase. We can tune: smaller batch windows, prefix caching, and proactive warm pools.
[02:26] Priya: When you say warm pools, do you mean reserved Dedicated instances?
[02:29] Diego: Yes — Dedicated capacity gives you reserved GPU pools that reduce cold-starts and let us guarantee lower variance. Hosted can be fast for many customers but at very high or highly bursty concurrency you'll see more queueing or fallback to larger batches.
[02:41] Sofia: Cost is a big factor. If Dedicated is required for the latency SLOs, what's the ballpark difference in unit cost vs Hosted?
[02:48] Olivia: We'll send detailed pricing, but high-level: Dedicated involves base reserved capacity (monthly commit) plus per-token or per-hour usage for bursts. Hosted is pure usage. For high sustained qps Dedicated tends to be more economical. We'll include sample math in the doc.
[02:59] Liam: Back to benchmarking — what would you need from our side to reproduce our peak behavior?
[03:03] Diego: Two things: 1) anonymized inference traces with sequence length histogram, qps over time, and concurrency patterns; 2) a small sample payload set (prompts) representative of typical messages — obfuscated PII is fine. With those we can run a token/sec and streaming p95 benchmark on a mirrored Dedicated config, and show token/sec, p50/p95/p99, and streaming first-token latency.
[03:20] Priya: Can you also show tail behavior under a 5–10 minute sustained surge? That's the painful case for us.
[03:25] Diego: Absolutely. We'll run surge scenarios: step increases to peak concurrency and sustained bursts, and measure queueing, coldstart rate, and model fallback latencies.
[03:33] Olivia: One caveat — for Private on-prem we need to coordinate on hardware. If you want the on-prem flavor we ship configs for common GPUs; if you have existing infra we can advise capacity numbers.
[03:43] Sofia: We may have spare H100s in an on-prem colocation later this year, but for the pilot we prefer Hosted or Dedicated in EU. We want to avoid double-networking hops — demo should be close to our PoPs.
[03:53] Liam: Two more tech asks: 1) Does Redwood support streaming SSE (server-sent events) and websockets parity? 2) For KV cache, how is multi-tenant cache isolation handled?
[04:03] Diego: Yes for streaming — Redwood's API supports chunked streaming and websockets in the hosted and dedicated runtimes. For KV cache, Dedicated gives you isolated cache maps per customer, and we can pin model versions to avoid cross-tenant eviction effects. Private gives you full control.
[04:16] Priya: Security questions — SOC2, ISO, SSO integration, audit logs, and KMS. We need to know whether logs contain prompt text, and retention windows.
[04:26] Olivia: We are SOC2 Type II. Audit logs can be configured to mask prompts; for regulated workloads we recommend Private with customer-managed KMS and audit retention on your side. We'll send the security whitepaper.
[04:36] Priya: Great. Also, can Redwood route requests by policy? We might want to route low-latency traffic to Dedicated and fallback to hosted cheaper models for non-critical paths.
[04:44] Diego: Yes, smart routing is supported. You can set policy by latency, cost, region, or tenant. We also support automatic fallback to compatible quantized variants when capacity is constrained.
[04:54] Sofia: How about canary or rollout behavior for model upgrades? We need to keep route decisions stable during rollouts.
[05:00] Diego: We support canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic rollback on quality regressions defined by your eval set. For critical production flows we'll recommend conservative rollout percentages and pre-flight checks.
[05:09] Liam: Let's talk numbers — if we aim for 250 concurrent streaming sessions in EU during normal peaks, and up to 400 during surges, what's the expected tokens/sec throughput for the Dedicated pool?
[05:19] Diego: Rough estimate depends on model throughput: say 13B quantized gives ~70–120 tokens/sec per GPU stream for streaming workloads on optimized kernels; with concurrent streams multiplexed across N GPUs and continuous batching we can approximate total tokens/sec = tokens/sec_per_gpu * number_gpus * utilization. For 250–400 concurrency we often recommend starting with 4–8 GPU Dedicated pool for pilot and scale from there based on measured token/sec. We'll run a profiling pass to produce exact numbers.
[05:40] Olivia: We'll produce a sizing recommendation after the benchmark. For now, expect the benchmark report to include recommended GPUs, expected p95 ranges, and cost estimates.
[05:47] Priya: Can Redwood's runtime keep session affinity so streaming sessions don't rehydrate KV cache each request?
[05:53] Diego: Yes — session affinity and sticky routing help preserve KV cache. We also support pre-warming caches for canary users.
[05:59] Sofia: About token accounting — we want per-route token-level cost breakdowns for finance reporting.
[06:04] Olivia: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns by route and model. We'll demo that during the pilot kickoff.
[06:12] Liam: Any limits on streaming throughput per connection? We expect some clients to throttle to save battery; others will keep long-open streams.
[06:20] Diego: We allow long-lived streams; connection limits are configurable on Dedicated and Private. We'll share recommended TCP/TLS settings for mobile users.
[06:27] Priya: For the benchmark, can you simulate 10–15% of requests that require 700–800 token outputs? The tail matters.
[06:33] Diego: Yes — include those in the trace export and we'll drive the bench with realistic sequence length mixes.
[06:39] (brief cross-talk)
[06:42] Olivia: Let's capture deliverables and timeline — Diego will draft the bench plan and Olivia will send pricing + SLA. Customer to provide traces by Monday. Pilot kickoff week after that.
[06:51] Priya: Sounds good. A couple of open concerns: routing failover between EU/NA if a region is saturated, and cold starts for infrequent models.
[06:58] Diego: For failover we can replicate model variants in multiple regions and route by policy with graceful degrade. For cold starts we use warm pools plus fast model load paths; dedicated reserved capacity minimizes coldstart exposure.
[07:08] Liam: Do you support model quantization recommendations? We plan to quantize but worry about quality regressions.
[07:14] Diego: Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations by workload and will run quality regressions against your eval prompts. We can tie regressions to alerting during pilot.
[07:22] Sofia: One more — network egress TS cost for a lot of token streaming out of EU is a cost center we need to understand.
[07:28] Olivia: We'll include egress estimates in the pricing spreadsheet. Also options: colocate inference in your VPC or on-prem for lower egress.
[07:35] Priya: Good. Anything else technically blocking the pilot?
[07:39] Diego: Not from Redwood's side. We'll just need the traces, sample prompts, and confirmation of pilot region and model family.
[07:46] Priya: We'll try to provide the artifacts by Monday.
[07:49] Olivia: Perfect. I'll summarize and email the plan: benchmark objectives, data list, estimated GPU sizing, and dates.
[07:55] (15-minute marker—conversation shifts to more granular questions)
[22:10] Liam: Quick question — how do you measure streaming first-token p95? Is that from request arrival at Redwood or from our edge?
[22:17] Diego: We can measure both. For the benchmark we'll instrument client-side timing (first-byte or first-token seen in client), and server-side timings (request received, model start, token emit). That gives a full breakdown.
[22:27] Priya: Excellent. We want the client-side numbers for our SLA.
[22:30] Diego: We'll collect that.
[22:33] Sofia: For Dedicated, what's the expected maintenance window behavior? We need near continuous availability during business hours.
[22:39] Olivia: We offer scheduled maintenance windows and can set SLAs for Dedicated tenants. We'll map that out in the SLA doc.
[22:45] Priya: Anything about model fallback quality? If we fallback to a quantized variant, what metrics do you provide to detect quality degradation?
[22:51] Diego: We run preflight evals and monitor production quality via your eval prompts and A/B comparisons. Alerts can be based on perplexity proxies or custom classifiers on output drift.
[22:59] (closing)
[23:05] Olivia: Thanks everyone — I'll send the email with next steps and Diego will attach the benchmark run plan. Any final questions?
[23:10] Priya: No, that's it. Thanks both.
[23:13] Liam: Thanks.
[23:15] Sofia: Thanks.

Recap (auto): Redwood to run surge and streaming-focused benchmark on Dedicated mirror using HighTide traces; customer to deliver traces and confirm region/model; Redwood to send pricing and pilot plan. Action items listed.
